title: One byte and the cache is gone
intro: The same extraction prompt, run twice: the second call reads 8,700 tokens from cache and costs a third as much. Then someone adds a date line to the top of the system prompt, and nothing errors.

provenance.source: a narrated UCC extraction service; token counts, hit rates, and prices are plausible inventions, not measurements

foot: The mechanism here is M19's Prefix Match: How Caching Actually Works — tools → system → messages, with the breakpoint at the end of the stable block.

steps.title: Call 1 — you pay for the rules
narrative: The extraction service reads one UCC filing per call and returns the debtor name as JSON. Its context is 11,340 tokens: 1,900 of tool definitions, 6,800 of rules and few-shot examples, and 2,640 of actual filing text.

On the first call the whole prefix is processed from scratch and written to cache — you pay a premium of roughly 1.25x on the cached portion for the privilege. cache_read_input_tokens comes back zero, as it should.
steps.youDo: Put a cache_control breakpoint at the end of your own system block, then print both cache_creation_input_tokens and cache_read_input_tokens from the response.

terminal.text: extract("FILING 2024-FL-0012345 DEBTOR: ACME LOGISTICS & DISTRIBUTION, L.L.C. ...")

before.title: COLD — the rules processed from scratch

view.question: extract the debtor from 2024-FL-0012345
view.verdictNote: correct extraction, and a cache write premium of about 1.25x on the 8,700-token prefix

steps.title: Call 2 — same rules, new filing
narrative: The next filing arrives. The tool definitions and the system block are byte-identical, so the model matches the prefix and reuses the processed tokens at roughly a tenth of the input price. Only the 2,640 tokens of new filing text are processed fresh.
The receipt barely changes shape and the cost falls from $0.0432 to $0.0132. 77% of the input was read from cache — and that number is the one you check, not the one you assume.
steps.claudeSays: Nothing about my answer changed. What changed is that 8,700 tokens of it were already computed.

terminal.text: extract("FILING 2024-FL-0019988 DEBTOR: REDLINE FREIGHT CAPITAL LLC ...")

view.question: extract the debtor from 2024-FL-0019988
view.verdictNote: same tokens in the window, 69% less money, because 8,700 of them were already processed

steps.title: Multiply it by fifty thousand
narrative: The pipeline processes 50,000 filings a day and the rules are identical for every one of them. Without caching that is 50,000 re-readings of the same 8,700 tokens — a tax you pay per call, forever.

With one breakpoint it becomes a single write followed by 49,999 reads. Same model, same prompt, same answers; the difference is $1,175 a day. This is why caching is the highest-leverage cost move in the module.
steps.youDo: Multiply your own stable prefix size by your daily call volume before you optimize anything else. The number usually settles the argument.

items.label: cached prefix
items.note: one write, then 49,999 reads at about a tenth of input price

steps.title: One byte moves
narrative: Support asked which build answered a given filing, so someone helpfully added a freshness stamp to the top of the system prompt: Current date: 2026-08-28. It is 6 tokens, it is accurate, and it changes the prefix bytes on every call that crosses midnight — and in the version that shipped, on every call at all.
Caching is a prefix match. A change anywhere in the cached span invalidates everything after it, so the entire 8,700-token block is now processed fresh on every single request. Cache read: 0%.
steps.claudeSays: The line is at the top, which is the worst possible place. If it had gone in the user message after the breakpoint, the cache would still be intact.

terminal.text: +  "Current date: 2026-08-28\n"       # 6 tokens, top of the cached prefix
extract("FILING 2024-FL-0021077 DEBTOR: NORTHBAY MARINE SUPPLY INC ...")

steps.title: Nothing errors — that is the problem
narrative: No exception, no warning, no failed test. Extraction quality is unchanged, latency creeps up a little, and the invoice goes up by $1,500 a day for twelve days before anyone looks.

It is worse than having no cache at all. Every call now writes a prefix nobody will ever read, so you pay the 1.25x write premium 50,000 times a day — $2,160 against the $1,835 you would have spent with caching switched off entirely.

The only signal is the one the API already hands you. Assert on it: if cache_read_input_tokens is zero on the second identical call, your prefix is not stable and you want that to be a red build, not a line item.
steps.youDo: Write a two-call smoke test — same system block, two different user messages — and assert the second response has a non-zero cache read.

steps.title: The cacheability rule
narrative: Render order is fixed — tools, then system, then messages — so cacheability is entirely a question of what you put where. Anything that varies per call must sit after the breakpoint, and anything stable must sit before it with nothing volatile in front.

The silent invalidators are always the same short list: a timestamp, a request or user ID, an unsorted JSON dump, a randomly ordered tool array. Freeze them, sort them, or move them into the user message.
Static content first, volatile content last, one breakpoint at the seam, and a hit-rate assertion in CI. That is the whole discipline.
steps.youDo: Print your own prompt as bytes on two consecutive calls and diff them. Everything that differs before your breakpoint is costing you the cache.

cells: date / request id, if you need them

views.text: Static first, volatile last, one breakpoint at the seam. Then verify with cache_read_input_tokens rather than assuming — a cache miss is invisible in the output and only shows up on the invoice.
